Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Workplace safety in hazardous environments like construction sites and industrial plants is crucial to prevent accidents and injuries. One of the most important safety measures is ensuring workers wear safety helmets, which protect against head injuries from falling objects and machinery. Non-compliance with helmet regulations increases the risk of serious injuries or fatalities, making effective monitoring essential, especially in large-scale operations where manual oversight is prone to errors and inefficiency.

To overcome these challenges, SafeGuard Corp plans to develop an automated image analysis system capable of detecting whether workers are wearing safety helmets. This system will improve safety enforcement, ensuring compliance and reducing the risk of head injuries. By automating helmet monitoring, SafeGuard aims to enhance efficiency, scalability, and accuracy, ultimately fostering a safer work environment while minimizing human error in safety oversight.

Objective¶

As a data scientist at SafeGuard Corp, you are tasked with developing an image classification model that classifies images into one of two categories:

  • With Helmet: Workers wearing safety helmets.
  • Without Helmet: Workers not wearing safety helmets.

Data Description¶

The dataset consists of 4125 images, divided into two categories:

  • With Helmet: 3161 images showing workers wearing helmets.
  • Without Helmet: 964 images showing workers not wearing helmets.

Dataset Characteristics:

  • Variations in Conditions: Images include diverse environments such as construction sites, factories, and industrial settings, with variations in lighting, angles, and worker postures to simulate real-world conditions.
  • Worker Activities: Workers are depicted in different actions such as standing, using tools, or moving, ensuring robust model learning for various scenarios.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Adjust this if your label column has a different name
label_col = 'label'  # e.g. could be 'class' or 'category'

unique_classes = labels[label_col].unique()
n_classes = len(unique_classes)

# Set up a grid of subplots
n_cols = 4
n_rows = int(np.ceil(n_classes / n_cols))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(4 * n_cols, 4 * n_rows))
axes = axes.flatten()

for i, cls in enumerate(unique_classes):
    # Get indices of all images belonging to this class
    class_indices = labels[labels[label_col] == cls].index

    # Pick one at random
    random_idx = np.random.choice(class_indices)

    # Plot it
    axes[i].imshow(images[random_idx].astype('uint8'))
    axes[i].set_title(f"Class: {cls}\n(index {random_idx})")
    axes[i].axis('off')

# Hide any unused subplots
for j in range(i + 1, len(axes)):
    axes[j].axis('off')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Utility Functions¶

In [26]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using statsmodels
def model_performance_classification(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # checking which probabilities are greater than threshold
    pred = model.predict(predictors).reshape(-1)>0.5

    target = target.to_numpy().reshape(-1)


    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred, average='micro')  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred, average='micro')  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred, average='micro')  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame({"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1 Score": f1,},index=[0],)

    return df_perf
In [27]:
def plot_confusion_matrix(model,predictors,target,ml=False):
    """
    Function to plot the confusion matrix

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    ml: To specify if the model used is an sklearn ML model or not (True means ML model)
    """

    # checking which probabilities are greater than threshold
    pred = model.predict(predictors).reshape(-1)>0.5

    target = target.to_numpy().reshape(-1)

    # Plotting the Confusion Matrix using confusion matrix() function which is also predefined tensorflow module
    confusion_matrix = tf.math.confusion_matrix(target,pred)
    f, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
    sns.heatmap(
        confusion_matrix,
        annot=True,
        linewidths=.4,
        fmt="d",
        square=True,
        ax=ax
    )
    plt.show()
In [28]:
from tensorflow.keras.callbacks import EarlyStopping

# Shared early-stopping callback reused across all four models below: stops
# training once validation loss stops improving and restores the best weights.
early_stop = EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=5, restore_best_weights=True)

def plot_training_curves(history, title):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

    axes[0].plot(history.history['loss'], label='Train Loss')
    axes[0].plot(history.history['val_loss'], label='Val Loss')
    axes[0].set_title(f'{title} - Loss')
    axes[0].set_xlabel('Epoch')
    axes[0].legend()

    axes[1].plot(history.history['accuracy'], label='Train Accuracy')
    axes[1].plot(history.history['val_accuracy'], label='Val Accuracy')
    axes[1].set_title(f'{title} - Accuracy')
    axes[1].set_xlabel('Epoch')
    axes[1].legend()

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Model 1: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) from Scratch¶

In [68]:
tf.keras.backend.clear_session()

model_1 = Sequential([
    Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', input_shape=(200, 200, 3)),
    BatchNormalization(),
    MaxPooling2D((2, 2)),

    Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'),
    BatchNormalization(),
    MaxPooling2D((2, 2)),

    Conv2D(128, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'),
    BatchNormalization(),
    MaxPooling2D((2, 2)),

    Flatten(),
    Dense(128, activation='relu'),
    Dropout(0.3),
    Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
])

model_1.compile(optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.001), loss='binary_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
model_1.summary()

In [110]:
model_2 = Sequential()

# Adding the convolutional part of the VGG16 model from above
model_2.add(vgg_model)

# Flattening the output of the VGG16 model because it is from a convolutional layer
model_2.add(Flatten())

# Adding a dense output layer
model_2.add(Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'))

Model 3: Transfer Learning with VGG-16 (Base + FFNN)¶

In [119]:
tf.keras.backend.clear_session()

vgg_model_3 = VGG16(weights='imagenet', include_top=False, input_shape=(200, 200, 3))
for layer in vgg_model_3.layers:
    layer.trainable = False

model_3 = Sequential()
model_3.add(vgg_model_3)
model_3.add(Flatten())
model_3.add(Dense(256, activation='relu')) # Added an additional Dense layer
model_3.add(Dropout(0.3))
model_3.add(Dense(128, activation='relu'))
model_3.add(Dropout(0.3))
model_3.add(Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'))

model_3.compile(optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.0001), loss='binary_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
model_3.summary()

Model 4: Transfer Learning with VGG-16 (Base + FFNN + Data Augmentation)¶

  • In most of the real-world case studies, it is challenging to acquire a large number of images and then train CNNs.
  • To overcome this problem, one approach we might consider is Data Augmentation.

  • CNNs have the property of translational invariance, which means they can recognise an object even if its appearance shifts translationally in some way. - Taking this attribute into account, we can augment the images using the techniques listed below

    • Horizontal Flip (should be set to True/False)
    • Vertical Flip (should be set to True/False)
    • Height Shift (should be between 0 and 1)
    • Width Shift (should be between 0 and 1)
    • Rotation (should be between 0 and 180)
    • Shear (should be between 0 and 1)
    • Zoom (should be between 0 and 1) etc.

Remember, data augmentation should not be used in the validation/test data set.

In [125]:
tf.keras.backend.clear_session()

vgg_model_4 = VGG16(weights='imagenet', include_top=False, input_shape=(200, 200, 3))
for layer in vgg_model_4.layers:
    layer.trainable = False

model_4 = Sequential()
model_4.add(vgg_model_4)
model_4.add(Flatten())
model_4.add(Dense(256, activation='relu'))
model_4.add(Dropout(0.5))
model_4.add(Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'))

model_4.compile(optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.0001), loss='binary_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
model_4.summary()

Final Model Selection¶

Based on the performance metrics on the validation set, we can compare the models:

  • Model 1 (CNN from Scratch): Achieved a validation accuracy of 90.78%. This custom CNN provides a strong baseline performance.
  • Model 2 (VGG16 Base): Achieved a validation accuracy of 86.65%. This model uses the VGG16 convolutional base with a simple classification head.
  • Model 3 (VGG16 Base + FFNN): Achieved the highest validation accuracy of 91.99%. This model leverages a pre-trained VGG16 base combined with a custom fully connected neural network.
  • Model 4 (VGG16 Base + FFNN + Data Augmentation): Achieved a validation accuracy of 91.26%. This model is similar to Model 3 but incorporates data augmentation during training.

Conclusion:

Model 3 (VGG16 Base + FFNN) demonstrates the strongest performance on the validation set, exhibiting the highest accuracy among all tested models. Its ability to effectively utilize pre-trained features from VGG16 and fine-tune them with a robust custom classification head makes it the most effective for this helmet detection task. Model 4, with data augmentation, also shows strong performance, suggesting that data augmentation can further enhance generalization, even if it yielded a slightly lower accuracy than Model 3 in this specific run.

Actionable Insights & Recommendations¶

  • Best Performing Model (Model 3 - VGG16 Base + FFNN): Model 3 demonstrated superior performance, achieving a validation accuracy of 91.99% and a test accuracy of 89.83%. This model effectively leveraged the pre-trained feature extraction capabilities of VGG16 while adapting to the specific task with a custom fully connected neural network (FFNN) and appropriate dropout layers for regularization.
  • Strong Baseline with Custom CNN (Model 1): The custom CNN (Model 1) provided a good baseline, achieving a validation accuracy of 90.78%. This indicates that a well-designed custom architecture can perform competitively, although it might require more training data or deeper tuning than a transfer learning approach.
  • Benefit of Custom Classification Head (Model 2 vs. Model 3): Model 2 (VGG16 Base with a simple output layer) yielded a validation accuracy of 86.65%. The significant improvement seen in Model 3 (VGG16 Base + FFNN) underscores the importance of a custom, trainable classification head built on top of the frozen VGG16 base. This allows the model to learn more complex relationships specific to the helmet detection task.
  • Impact of Data Augmentation (Model 4): Model 4, which incorporated data augmentation, achieved a validation accuracy of 91.26%. While slightly lower than Model 3 in this specific run, data augmentation is crucial for improving model generalization, especially with limited datasets. Further experimentation with augmentation parameters and training epochs could potentially enhance its performance and robustness.
  • Class Imbalance: The dataset exhibits a class imbalance (approximately 76% 'With Helmet' vs. 23% 'Without Helmet'). While the models achieved high overall accuracy, this imbalance might lead to a bias towards the majority class. It is important to monitor precision and recall for the 'Without Helmet' class, as false negatives in this category are critical for safety applications.

Recommendations:¶

  • Deploy Model 3: Based on its consistent strong performance on both validation and test sets, Model 3 (VGG16 Base + FFNN) is the recommended model for deployment.
  • Focus on 'Without Helmet' Metrics: During deployment, closely monitor specific metrics such as recall and precision for the 'Without Helmet' class. This will ensure that the model is effective at identifying safety non-compliance, where false negatives could have significant safety implications.
  • Data Collection and Balancing: Prioritize collecting more 'Without Helmet' images to naturally reduce the class imbalance. Alternatively, consider implementing advanced techniques for handling class imbalance, such as using weighted loss functions, oversampling the minority class, or undersampling the majority class during training.
  • Hyperparameter Optimization: While Model 3 performs well, further fine-tuning of its hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate schedules, dropout rates, number of neurons in dense layers) could lead to marginal improvements in performance or faster convergence.
  • Explore Other Architectures: For future iterations or more complex scenarios, consider experimenting with other state-of-the-art pre-trained CNN architectures (e.g., ResNet, EfficientNet, MobileNet) to potentially achieve higher accuracy, better efficiency, or suitability for deployment on edge devices.

Power Ahead!
